subject: Culture
title: Inti Raymi Sun Festival
description: A micro-lesson that makes Inti Raymi Sun Festival usable.

hook.text: Every June, Cusco reenacts an Incan ceremony to honor the sun god. Thousands gather at the ruins.

buildup.text: Inti Raymi celebrated the winter solstice in the Southern Hemisphere and asked the sun to return.

discovery.text: The Spanish banned it in 1572 as part of their campaign to destroy Incan religion.

twist.text: In 1944, local artists revived the ceremony from historical accounts. The modern version is a reconstruction.

climax.text: A festival destroyed by colonizers was rebuilt from memory. Culture can survive its own erasure.

punchline.text: They banned the sun festival. The sun came back anyway.

quiz.question: When was the original Inti Raymi banned by Spanish colonizers?

details.summary: Inti Raymi was the Inca Empire's most important ceremony — a winter solstice celebration honoring the sun god Inti. Spanish colonizers banned it in 1572, but it was revived in 1944 and is now Peru's second-largest festival, drawing thousands to Cusco each June.
details.whyItMatters: Inti Raymi's ban and revival illustrate colonialism's attempt to erase indigenous culture and the power of cultural recovery movements. Its modern celebration is an act of decolonial reclamation.
takeaways: Inti Raymi honored the Inca sun god during the winter solstice
Spanish colonizers banned the festival in 1572
It was revived in 1944 and draws thousands of visitors annually

faq.question: What happened during the original Inti Raymi?
faq.answer: The Inca emperor led ceremonies at Sacsayhuamán fortress above Cusco. Llamas were sacrificed, chicha (corn beer) was offered to the sun, and elaborate dances and processions honored Inti.

faq.question: How was Inti Raymi revived?
faq.answer: In 1944, Cusqueño writer and actor Faustino Espinoza Navarro reconstructed the ceremony using Spanish colonial chronicles that had described it in detail before banning it.
